sections.html:
For Alabama property tax, a homestead is a single-family, owner-occupied dwelling plus the land with it, up to 160 acres. You must live there as your primary residence on the first day of the tax year for which you ask for the exemption.

That wording bites when you are selling. A house left empty after a move, a rental, or a home held by heirs who live elsewhere does not fit it. A house the owner lives in does, and the owner may qualify for a lower assessed value or, for some older and disabled owners, a bigger break. The legal text sits in Title 40 of the Alabama Code, sections 9-19 through 9-21, and the Department of Revenue publishes a homestead page plus yearly memoranda on the income tests.

sections.h2: The homestead types, H-1 through H-4
sections.html:
Alabama sorts homestead relief into four named types, labeled H-1 through H-4 under Act 2013-295. Age, income and disability decide which one fits an owner.

TypeWho qualifiesBenefit
H-1Owners under 65 who are not disabled$4,000 of assessed value on the state portion and $2,000 of assessed value on the county portion
H-2Owners 65 or older with adjusted gross income under $12,000 on the latest state return, or owners retired because of permanent and total disabilityExempt from the state portion, plus $5,000 of assessed value on the county portion, school district tax included
H-3 (age 65+)Owners 65 or older with net taxable income of $12,000 or less on the combined federal returnExempt from all ad valorem taxes
H-3 (disabled)Owners who are permanently and totally disabledExempt from all ad valorem taxes, with no income limit
H-4Owners 65 or older with income above $12,000 on the latest Alabama returnExempt from the state portion, plus the regular $2,000 assessed-value exemption on county taxes

These figures are assessed values, not market values. Alabama assesses residential property at a fraction of market value, so a few thousand dollars of assessed value removes a much larger slice of the price from the tax base.

sections.h2: How state, county and school taxes differ
sections.html:
Relief is applied separately to the state, county and school district parts of the bill, which is why two neighbors of different ages can see very different results.

On the state side, owners who are not 65 get up to $4,000 of assessed value off, with no income limit. Owners 65 or older, owners with a permanent and total disability, and blind owners have no maximum assessed value on the state exemption, again with no income limit and the same 160-acre ceiling.

The county side varies more. Counties, municipalities and other taxing authorities may grant their own exemption of up to $4,000 in assessed value, and county school tax is collected on some categories and not others. The mix depends on the county and on the owner. A seller who wants to know what a buyer will pay should call the local assessing office instead of assuming the statewide minimum.

You apply at your local county office, not with the state. All property tax other than public utility property is assessed and collected through the 67 county tax offices.

  • Be ready to show that you own the house and live in it as your primary residence.
  • For the age-based types, bring proof of age and, where the type has an income limit, the tax return that year's memorandum names.
  • For disability, a doctor completes a physician's affidavit verifying permanent and total disability.
  • Ask the office which type it has on file for you.

County office contacts are listed on the Department of Revenue site, and the Property Tax Division at 334-242-1525 can help if you cannot tell which office handles your parcel.

Alabama also has a combined state, county and city principal residence exemption under Title 40, section 9-21. It covers owners 65 or older with income of no more than $12,000 on the combined federal return, and owners who are permanently and totally disabled at any age.

Both groups get no maximum assessed value, a 160-acre land limit, and no county school tax. The disabled category has no income limit. The relief closely matches what the H-3 type describes.

sections.h2: What happens to the exemption when you sell
sections.html:
Do not guess about a mid-year sale. Call the county office to ask how your sale date affects the current-year bill. The firm rule is the occupancy test: the owner must live in the home as a primary residence on the first day of the tax year.

That test points to a practical split. If you owned and lived in the house on that date, your exemption for the year turned on your occupancy, and a buyer who moves in later starts the process with the county office. A buyer who plans to rent or flip the house will not meet the occupancy test, so an investor should price the property at the tax level without an exemption.

  • Ask the county office how a sale date affects your current-year bill.
  • Check the title company's statement for how property tax is split between seller and buyer.
  • Keep your copy of the exemption approval in case the title company asks for it.

sections.h2: Inherited a house? Plan for the tax bill
sections.html:
An heir who does not live in the inherited house does not meet the occupancy wording, so the decedent's exemption should not be assumed to continue. If the previous owner was 65 or older and paid little or no tax, the first bill after the death can look much higher.

Taxes are due October 1 and delinquent after December 31, and the County Revenue Commissioner is not required to mail tax notices. A bill that goes unpaid during a slow estate can become a larger problem, so check the account with the county early.

Heirs who want to skip repairs, carrying costs and uncertainty sometimes sell as-is. A cash buyer can close on your timeline and handle the cleanup, which is one way to stop the tax clock running against you. You can compare options at your own pace, and you owe nothing if you decline an offer.

The tax cycle runs on a short timetable, and a homestead exemption lowers the amount owed without moving any of these dates.

  • October 1: taxes are due.
  • January 1: taxes are delinquent.
  • February: delinquent accounts go to the probate court.
  • March: the probate court meets.
  • April: property is advertised for sale.
  • May: tax sale.

Add the day you list or sign a sales contract, since that date drives how the bill is split.

One rule differs for manufactured homes. Owners over 65 are exempt from the registration fee on an owner-occupied manufactured home, though they still pay the $5 issuance fee.

That is separate from the homestead types above, and it matters if you are selling a manufactured home on land you own. Ask the county office which fees and exemptions apply to the home and which apply to the land, since the two can be billed differently.

faqs.q: Who qualifies for the Alabama homestead exemption?
faqs.a: An owner of a single-family home who lives in it as a primary residence on the first day of the tax year, on up to 160 acres. The amount depends on age, income and disability status, and the types run from H-1 through H-4.

faqs.q: How much is the basic exemption for owners under 65?
faqs.a: H-1 owners get $4,000 of assessed value off the state portion and $2,000 off the county portion. Counties and other taxing authorities may grant up to $4,000 of assessed value on their own.

faqs.q: Do I apply with the state or the county?
faqs.a: With your county office. The Department of Revenue publishes the rules, but county offices assess and collect the tax.

faqs.q: When are Alabama property taxes due?
faqs.a: October 1, and they are delinquent after December 31. The County Revenue Commissioner does not have to mail a bill, so you owe the tax whether or not a statement arrives.

faqs.q: Can I keep my homestead exemption after I sell?
faqs.a: Ask the county office about a mid-year sale. A buyer must apply for their own exemption, and the occupancy test looks at who lives in the home on the first day of the tax year.
